newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs seen rising on investors' flight to quality.
newsitem.headline: JGBs seen rising on investors' flight to quality.

text.p: Safe haven buying by local investors fleeing from fragile corporate bonds has made long-term Japanese government bonds (JGBs) the current market favourite, market sources said on Thursday.
Investors are extremely cautious about riskier investments such as corporate bonds with credit ratings of under triple B plus, as concerns mount over Japan"s bad loan problem.
Market participants said that this has shifted attention to the less shaky JGBs, keeping their yields from rising.
"There is a strong belief that interest rates cannot be raised in the near future," said one market source. "So people are fleeing to quality and buying long-term JGBs," he said.

Japan"s current rock-bottom short-term money rates and weakness in the stock market make it difficult for investors to find places to park their funds, but they are also wary of buying high-yielding corporate bonds, sources said.

The lack of interest has kept some corporate bonds with low credit ratings from trading at all, including those issued by long-term credit banks, non-bank financial institutions and real estate and construction firms, they said.

The spread between the London interbank offered rate (LIBOR) and the offer yield of such bonds has widened because the holders seek higher liquidity and prefer to replace them with other bonds with higher credit ratings, they said.
"Investors are very eager to buy corporate bonds with credit ratings of double A or above," said Yasunari Ueno, chief market economist at Fuji Securities Co Ltd.
"But they are cautious about taking the risk of buying other bonds," Ueno added.

Since the key 182nd 10-year JGB yield hit a record low of 2.330 percent in December last year, it had risen only to 2.635 percent before falling to the current level. The yield stood at 2.405 percent at midday on Thursday.

This is often the case ahead of the end-March fiscal book closing period here, but some sources say the widening spread can also be attributed to concerns over possible default by some of the debt-ridden companies.

Falling asset prices since 1990 have saddled Japan"s banking system with huge bad loans, and many companies, especially in the financial and real estate sectors, are still struggling to get out from under them.
Unlike stocks, bonds are repaid when they mature, but if the issuer of a corporate bond were to collapse, the principle of the bond may not be returned in full.
The secondary market of bank debentures and corporate bonds shows that there are investors who are eager to sell their holdings at a lower price than when they bought.

Construction firm Fujita Corp"s 5.3 percent straight bond due October 1998 was last traded at a yield of 5.6 percent on Friday. The bond, rated triple B plus by a local credit rating agency, was offered at a yield of 5.69 percent late on Wednesday, about 500 basis points above LIBOR.
Another building firm, JDC Corp"s 4.5 percent straight bond due September 1999, rated triple B, was offered at a yield of 5.0 percent, about 400 basis points above LIBOR.
"Bonds issued by certain industries now are too fragile a market for us to tap," said a second market source, who also declined to be named.

"Some construction firms are barely surviving on a life-support system, but it could be disconnected at any time," he added. "For example, when banks decide not to support them anymore or when the government reduces public spending from April 1 (beginning of the fiscal year)," he added.
